# Overview

This report documents the exploratory data analysis (EDA) and quality control (QC) of the
**RNA-seq data of the TCGA-BRCA training set**. The aim is to understand the structure of the
data, remove uninformative genes, detect atypical patients and identify technical factors that
must be considered in the models (PCA, multi-omics integration, machine learning).

**Data**

- Input: `data/data_split/rna.train.rds`, with one row per patient and one column per gene, and the clinical data `clin.train.rds`.
- Values: RSEM gene-level counts transformed as **log2(CPM + 1)** in `01_data_preparation.R`. CPM corrects for sequencing depth using only each sample's own total, so it was safe to compute before the train/test split.
- Output (written by `02_qc_rnaseq.R`): the filtered genes (`rna.train.filtered.rds`) and the QC parameters (`rna_qc_params.rds`), used to apply exactly the same filter to the test set.

All decisions are made on the training set only. This report does not overwrite any file
(the saving step is shown but not run). Knit it from the project root with
`rmarkdown::render("01_data_preprocess/02_qc_rnaseq.Rmd")`.

# Setup

Packages, a common plot theme and two helper functions used in the report.

```{r}
library(matrixStats)   # fast row/column statistics on matrices
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r}
theme_qc <- function(base_size = 12) {
  theme_classic(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold"),
          plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = 9),
          legend.position = "top")
}
```

The barplot helper groups the proportion of zeros in bins (green = no zeros, blue = some zeros,
red = mostly zeros).

```{r}
plot_zero_bins <- function(zero_frac, title, x_lab, step = 0.05, max_frac = 1) {
  upper  <- seq(step, max_frac, by = step)
  breaks <- c(-Inf, 0, upper, if (max_frac < 1) Inf)
  labels <- c("0%", paste0(round(100 * (upper - step)), "-", round(100 * upper), "%"),
              if (max_frac < 1) paste0("> ", round(100 * max_frac), "%"))
  df <- as.data.frame(table(bin = cut(zero_frac, breaks = breaks, labels = labels)))
  df$pct <- df$Freq / sum(df$Freq)
  
  n_bins   <- nrow(df)
  high_lab <- if (max_frac < 1) paste0("> ", round(100 * max_frac), "% zeros") else "> 90% zeros"
  is_high  <- if (max_frac < 1) seq_len(n_bins) == n_bins else c(0, upper) > 0.9
  df$group <- factor(ifelse(seq_len(n_bins) == 1, "No zeros",
                            ifelse(is_high, high_lab, "Some zeros")),
                     levels = c("No zeros", "Some zeros", high_lab))
  
  ggplot(df, aes(bin, Freq, fill = group)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.8) +
    geom_text(data = subset(df, Freq > 0),
              aes(label = sprintf("%d\n(%.0f%%)", Freq, 100 * pct)),
              vjust = -0.2, size = 2.6, lineheight = 0.85) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("#1A9850", "#2C7FB8", "#D73027"), name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = sprintf("n = %d", length(zero_frac)),
         x = x_lab, y = "Count") +
    theme_qc() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
}
```

The robust z-score uses the median and the MAD instead of the mean and the SD, so that the
atypical values do not hide themselves by inflating the SD.

```{r}
robust_z <- function(x) (x - median(x)) / mad(x)
```

# Data loading

The data are read as a numeric matrix with patients in rows and genes in columns, and the
clinical data are put in the same patient order.

```{r}
path.x <- "./data/data_split"

df <- readRDS(file.path(path.x, "rna.train.rds"))
X  <- as.matrix(df[, colnames(df) != "patientID"])   # samples x genes
rownames(X) <- df$patientID
rm(df); gc()

clin <- readRDS(file.path(path.x, "clin.train.rds"))
clin <- clin[rownames(X), ]                         # same patients, same order

class(X); dim(X)
```

# Sanity checks

For log2(CPM + 1) data we expect no missing values, no duplicated patients or genes, no
negative values, a range from 0 to about 20, and non-integer values. Zeros are excluded from the
integer check because log2(0 + 1) = 0 is an integer even in transformed data.

```{r}
data.frame(
  check = c("Patients", "Genes", "Missing values", "Duplicated patients",
            "Duplicated genes", "Minimum value", "Maximum value", "Negative values",
            "Proportion of non-integer values (among non-zero values)",
            "Overall proportion of zeros"),
  value = c(nrow(X), ncol(X), sum(is.na(X)), sum(duplicated(rownames(X))),
            sum(duplicated(colnames(X))), round(min(X), 2), round(max(X), 2), sum(X < 0),
            round(mean(X[X != 0] != round(X[X != 0])), 3), round(mean(X == 0), 3))
)
```

# Zeros and uninformative genes

There are no missing values, so **zeros play the role of "not detected"** values. They are
analysed per gene and per patient.

```{r}
zero_gene   <- colMeans(X == 0)   # proportion of patients with zero, per gene
zero_sample <- rowMeans(X == 0)   # proportion of genes with zero, per patient
```

## Zeros per gene

In RNA-seq this distribution usually has an asymmetric U shape:

- most genes have **no zeros**: they are expressed in all patients;
- a group on the right is zero in almost all patients: genes not expressed in this tissue or below the detection limit;
- genes in between behave as "on/off": expressed in some patients but not in others. This can reflect real biology or detection noise for low-expressed genes.

```{r}
plot_zero_bins(zero_gene, "Zeros per gene", "Percentage of patients with value = 0")
```

## Zeros per patient

All patients should have a similar proportion of zeros. A patient with many more zeros than the
rest would suggest a sample with a global detection problem (e.g. low sequencing quality).

```{r}
plot_zero_bins(zero_sample, "Zeros per patient", "Percentage of genes with value = 0",
               step = 0.01, max_frac = 0.5)
```

## Expression level of detected values

The **mean of the non-zero values** of each gene tells how strongly a gene is expressed *when it
is detected*. If the distribution is bimodal, the low component is mostly detection noise and
the high component the clearly expressed genes. Genes with low expression and frequent zeros are removed (see Filtering below).

```{r, results = "hide"}
nz_mean <- apply(X, 2, function(x) if (any(x > 0)) mean(x[x > 0]) else 0)

# Data-driven threshold: minimum of the density between 1 and 7.
d      <- density(nz_mean)
search <- d$x > 1 & d$x < 7
nz_cut <- round(d$x[search][which.min(d$y[search])], 2)
nz_cut
```

## Filtering

Genes are removed if they carry no information or if they look like detection noise:

| Rule | Criterion | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Zero variance | SD = 0 | No information at all |
| Mostly zeros | zeros in > 90% of patients | Not expressed |
| Low expression **and** frequent zeros | non-zero mean below a data-derived threshold (minimum of the density of the non-zero means between 1 and 7 log2 CPM + 1) **and** zeros in ≥ 10% of patients | Typical pattern of detection noise |

Genes with low but **consistent** expression (below the threshold but detected in more than 90% of
patients) are **kept**: a stable low signal is unlikely to be noise. No filter on variance is
applied at this step: there is no natural cut-off, and the least variable genes are usually
well-expressed, stable genes rather than noise.

```{r}
gene_sd      <- colSds(X)
rm_zero_var  <- gene_sd == 0
rm_high_zero <- zero_gene > 0.9
rm_low_expr  <- nz_mean < nz_cut & zero_gene >= 0.1
remove       <- rm_zero_var | rm_high_zero | rm_low_expr

# Record of removed genes and the reason
filter_log <- data.frame(gene = colnames(X), nz_mean = nz_mean, zero_prop = zero_gene,
                         zero_var = rm_zero_var, high_zero = rm_high_zero,
                         low_expr = rm_low_expr, removed = remove)

X_filt <- X[, !remove]

data.frame(rule  = c("Zero variance", "Zeros in > 90% of patients",
                     "Low expression and frequent zeros", "Total removed (union)",
                     "Genes kept"),
           genes = c(sum(rm_zero_var), sum(rm_high_zero), sum(rm_low_expr),
                     sum(remove), ncol(X_filt)))
```

# Per-patient distributions

After normalisation, all patients should have similar distributions. A patient whose median or
spread is far from the rest (|robust z| > 3) is flagged (red).

```{r}
sample_stats <- data.frame(sample        = rownames(X_filt),
                           sample_median = rowMedians(X_filt),
                           iqr           = rowIQRs(X_filt))
sample_stats$z_median <- robust_z(sample_stats$sample_median)
sample_stats$z_iqr    <- robust_z(sample_stats$iqr)
sample_stats$flag     <- abs(sample_stats$z_median) > 3 | abs(sample_stats$z_iqr) > 3

long <- data.frame(sample = rep(rownames(X_filt), times = ncol(X_filt)),
                   value  = as.vector(X_filt))
long$sample <- factor(long$sample,
                      levels = sample_stats$sample[order(sample_stats$sample_median)])
long$flag   <- sample_stats$flag[match(long$sample, sample_stats$sample)]
```

## Boxplot per patient

Patients are ordered by their median. Well-aligned boxes indicate a good normalisation.

```{r}
ggplot(long, aes(sample, value, fill = flag)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.2, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey80", `TRUE` = "#D73027"), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Expression distribution per patient",
       subtitle = "Red = unusual median or spread (|robust z| > 3)",
       x = "Patient (ordered by median)", y = "log2(CPM + 1)") +
  theme_qc() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank())
```

## Density per patient

Each line is one patient. A curve with a different shape or clearly shifted would point to a
technical problem in that sample.

```{r}
ggplot(long, aes(value, group = sample, colour = flag)) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey75", `TRUE` = "#D73027"), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Density of expression values per patient",
       x = "log2(CPM + 1)", y = "Density") +
  theme_qc()

subset(sample_stats, flag)
rm(long); gc()
```

Patients flagged by their distribution (if any) are listed above. A flag here is not a reason to
remove a patient, but to look at it again in the next steps.

# Patient–patient correlation

Each pair of patients is compared through the Pearson correlation of their expression profiles.
The **standardized connectivity (Z.k)** (Oldham et al., 2012) summarises how strongly each
patient is connected to all others: correlations are transformed into connection strengths,
((1 + r) / 2)², summed per patient and standardised. Patients with **Z.k < −2** are weakly
correlated with the rest and are candidate outliers.

```{r}
C  <- cor(t(X_filt))                 # patient x patient
A  <- ((1 + C) / 2)^2
k  <- rowSums(A) - 1
zk <- (k - mean(k)) / sd(k)
med_cor <- apply(C, 1, function(x) median(x[x < 1]))

cor_stats <- data.frame(sample = rownames(X_filt), med_cor = med_cor, zk = zk)
cor_stats$group  <- ifelse(cor_stats$zk < -2, "Z.k < -2", "OK")
cor_stats$sample <- factor(cor_stats$sample, levels = cor_stats$sample[order(cor_stats$zk)])

ggplot(cor_stats, aes(sample, zk, colour = group)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -2, linetype = 2, colour = "#D73027") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("OK" = "#2C7FB8", "Z.k < -2" = "#D73027"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Standardized connectivity per patient",
       subtitle = "Patients below -2 are weakly correlated with the rest",
       x = "Patient (ordered by Z.k)", y = "Z.k") +
  theme_qc() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank())

summary(med_cor)
subset(cor_stats, zk < -2, select = c(sample, med_cor, zk))
```

The typical median correlation between patients is about `r round(median(med_cor), 2)`, and
`r sum(zk < -2)` patients have Z.k < −2. A low connectivity can be technical, but it can also
mean that the patient belongs to a small biological subgroup: in that case the patient still has
close neighbours with similar profiles, which is visible in the heatmap below.

## Correlation heatmap

Patients are ordered by hierarchical clustering, so that similar patients are next to each
other. Blocks along the diagonal are groups of similar patients; an isolated row and column with
low correlation to everyone would be a suspicious sample.

```{r}
hc  <- hclust(as.dist(1 - C), method = "average")
ord <- rownames(C)[hc$order]
heat_df <- data.frame(s1 = factor(rep(rownames(C), times = ncol(C)), levels = ord),
                      s2 = factor(rep(colnames(C), each = nrow(C)), levels = ord),
                      r  = as.vector(C))

ggplot(heat_df, aes(s1, s2, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Pearson r") +
  labs(title = "Patient-patient correlation (hierarchical clustering order)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())

rm(heat_df, A); gc()
```

# Gene distributions

## Randomly selected genes

Four random genes are shown from each tertile of mean expression (low, medium, high), to see
the typical shapes of the distributions at different expression levels.

```{r}
set.seed(20261013)
gene_mean <- colMeans(X_filt)
strata    <- cut(gene_mean, quantile(gene_mean, c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1)),
                 labels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"), include.lowest = TRUE)
pick <- unlist(lapply(split(colnames(X_filt), strata), sample, size = 4))

gene_df <- data.frame(gene    = factor(rep(pick, each = nrow(X_filt)), levels = pick),
                      stratum = rep(strata[match(pick, colnames(X_filt))], each = nrow(X_filt)),
                      value   = as.vector(X_filt[, pick]))

ggplot(gene_df, aes(value, fill = stratum)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ gene, scales = "free", ncol = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(n.breaks = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Low = "#7FCDBB", Medium = "#2C7FB8", High = "#253494"),
                    name = "Mean expression") +
  labs(title = "Distribution across patients of randomly selected genes",
       subtitle = "4 random genes per expression tertile",
       x = "log2(CPM + 1)", y = "Patients") +
  theme_qc(11) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

## Skewness

Skewness is reported descriptively, without classifying genes with conventional cut-offs. The red
lines mark Tukey's "far out" fences (Q1 − 3·IQR and Q3 + 3·IQR) computed on the skewness of all
genes, i.e. genes that are extreme *relative to the other genes*. Skewness matters mainly for
methods sensitive to tails (Pearson correlation, PCA, linear models); scaling does not change it.

```{r}
gene_skew <- apply(X_filt, 2, function(x) mean((x - mean(x))^3) / sd(x)^3)
q    <- quantile(gene_skew, c(0.25, 0.75))
lims <- c(q[1] - 3 * diff(q), q[2] + 3 * diff(q))

ggplot(data.frame(skew = gene_skew), aes(skew)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "#2C7FB8", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = lims, linetype = 2, colour = "#D73027") +
  labs(title = "Skewness of gene distributions",
       subtitle = sprintf("Grey = symmetric; red = Tukey far-out fences (%.2f, %.2f)",
                          lims[1], lims[2]),
       x = "Skewness", y = "Genes") +
  theme_qc()

head(round(sort(gene_skew[gene_skew < lims[1] | gene_skew > lims[2]]), 2), 30)
```

# Gene–gene correlation

A correlation matrix with all genes would need several GB of memory, so the **2,000 most
variable genes** are used. To judge whether the observed correlations exceed what is expected
by chance, a **permutation null** is built: each gene is shuffled independently across patients,
which keeps every gene's distribution but breaks all gene–gene relationships. The 95th
percentile of the null gives the chance level (red dashed line). Two views are shown:

- **All gene pairs**: the overall correlation structure.
- **Strongest correlation of each gene**: redundancy, i.e. how many genes have at least one highly correlated partner. Its chance level is higher, because the best of many candidates is always relatively high by chance.

```{r}
n_top     <- 2000
top_genes <- colnames(X_filt)[order(colVars(X_filt), decreasing = TRUE)[1:n_top]]
Xg        <- X_filt[, top_genes]

Cg <- cor(Xg)
r_pairs <- abs(Cg[upper.tri(Cg)])
diag(Cg) <- NA
max_r <- apply(abs(Cg), 1, max, na.rm = TRUE)

set.seed(1)
X_perm <- apply(Xg, 2, sample)
Cp <- cor(X_perm)
r_pairs_null <- abs(Cp[upper.tri(Cp)])
diag(Cp) <- NA
max_r_null <- apply(abs(Cp), 1, max, na.rm = TRUE)

cut_pairs <- quantile(r_pairs_null, 0.95)
cut_max   <- quantile(max_r_null, 0.95)

# Barplot of |r| in bins of 0.1, with the chance level as a dashed line
plot_cor_bins <- function(r, null_cut, title, y_lab) {
  breaks <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.1)
  df <- data.frame(mid  = head(breaks, -1) + 0.05,
                   Freq = as.vector(table(cut(r, breaks = breaks, include.lowest = TRUE))))
  df$pct   <- df$Freq / sum(df$Freq)
  df$level <- factor(ifelse(df$mid < 0.5, "|r| < 0.5", ifelse(df$mid < 0.8, "0.5 - 0.8", "> 0.8")),
                     levels = c("|r| < 0.5", "0.5 - 0.8", "> 0.8"))
  
  ggplot(df, aes(mid, Freq, fill = level)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.08) +
    geom_text(data = subset(df, Freq > 0),
              aes(label = sprintf("%d\n(%.1f%%)", Freq, 100 * pct)),
              vjust = -0.2, size = 2.6, lineheight = 0.85) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = null_cut, linetype = 2, colour = "#D73027") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("#1A9850", "#2C7FB8", "#D73027"), name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = breaks, limits = c(0, 1)) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) +
    labs(title = title,
         subtitle = sprintf("n = %d | dashed red line = chance level (95th percentile of permuted data = %.2f)",
                            length(r), null_cut),
         x = "|Pearson r|", y = y_lab) +
    theme_qc()
}

plot_cor_bins(r_pairs, cut_pairs,
              sprintf("Correlation between gene pairs (%d most variable genes)", n_top), "Gene pairs")
plot_cor_bins(max_r, cut_max,
              "Strongest correlation of each gene with any other gene", "Genes")

# Summary: proportion above chance and theoretical chance level 1.96 / sqrt(n - 3)
data.frame(measure = c("% gene pairs above chance level",
                       "% genes with a partner above chance level",
                       "Chance level (permutation)", "Chance level (theoretical)"),
           value   = round(c(100 * mean(r_pairs > cut_pairs), 100 * mean(max_r > cut_max),
                             cut_pairs, 1.96 / sqrt(nrow(Xg) - 3)), 3))

# Most correlated gene pairs
top_pairs <- which(abs(Cg) > 0.9 & upper.tri(Cg), arr.ind = TRUE)
head(data.frame(gene1 = rownames(Cg)[top_pairs[, 1]],
                gene2 = colnames(Cg)[top_pairs[, 2]],
                r     = round(Cg[top_pairs], 3)), 20)

rm(Cg, Cp, X_perm, Xg); gc()
```

- **`r round(100 * mean(r_pairs > cut_pairs), 1)`%** of the gene pairs are more correlated than expected by chance (5% would be expected without any structure).
- **`r round(100 * mean(max_r > cut_max), 1)`%** of the genes have at least one partner more correlated than expected by chance.
- Pairs with |r| > 0.9 (listed above) are highly redundant; a small number is normal.

A widespread but mostly moderate correlation structure means that collinearity is not a major
problem for the models, although methods that reduce dimensionality (PCA, penalised regression)
are still preferred.

# Extreme values per patient

A patient may look normal globally but have extreme values in many genes. For each gene, a robust
z-score is computed; values with **|robust z| > 5** are considered extreme (under normality,
essentially none would be expected in the whole matrix). The number of extreme values per
patient is compared with a Tukey far-out fence (Q3 + 3·IQR). Extreme expression can be
biological (e.g. gene amplifications or deletions in the tumour), so these values are
**flagged, not removed**.

```{r}
med <- colMedians(X_filt)
mdv <- colMads(X_filt)
ok  <- mdv > 0                      # genes with MAD = 0 cannot be standardised
Z   <- sweep(sweep(X_filt[, ok], 2, med[ok]), 2, mdv[ok], "/")

extreme   <- abs(Z) > 5
n_extreme <- rowSums(extreme)
q         <- quantile(n_extreme, c(0.25, 0.75))
fence     <- q[2] + 3 * diff(q)

ext_df <- data.frame(sample = names(n_extreme), n = n_extreme)
ext_df$sample <- factor(ext_df$sample, levels = ext_df$sample[order(ext_df$n)])
ext_df$flag   <- ext_df$n > fence

ggplot(ext_df, aes(sample, n, fill = flag)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = fence, linetype = 2, colour = "#D73027") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#2C7FB8", `TRUE` = "#D73027"), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Extreme values per patient",
       subtitle = sprintf("Genes with |robust z| > 5; dashed red line = Q3 + 3 IQR (%.1f)", fence),
       x = "Patient (ordered)", y = "Number of genes") +
  theme_qc() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank())

flagged_ext <- as.character(ext_df$sample[ext_df$flag])
data.frame(patient   = flagged_ext,
           n_extreme = n_extreme[flagged_ext],
           row.names = NULL)

# Overall proportion of extreme values
c(n_extreme_values = sum(extreme), pct = round(100 * mean(extreme), 3))

rm(Z, extreme); gc()
```

Overall, `r sum(n_extreme)` values (`r round(100 * sum(n_extreme) / (nrow(X_filt) * sum(ok)), 2)`%
of the matrix) are extreme, and `r sum(n_extreme > fence)` patients are above the fence.

# Principal component analysis

The PCA is computed on the filtered genes, **centred but not scaled**: all genes are on the same
log2(CPM + 1) scale, so the most variable genes (where most of the signal lies) carry more
weight.

```{r}
pca     <- prcomp(X_filt, center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)
var_exp <- pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2)
```

## Variance explained

Proportion of the total variance captured by each of the first 15 components.

```{r}
ggplot(data.frame(pc = 1:15, var = 100 * var_exp[1:15]), aes(pc, var)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2C7FB8") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", var)), vjust = -0.4, size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:15) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  labs(title = "Variance explained per principal component",
       x = "Principal component", y = "Variance explained (%)") +
  theme_qc()
```

## Data for the PCA plots

The PC scores are combined with the QC metrics of the previous sections (sample median,
proportion of zeros, connectivity, number of extreme values), the tissue source site (centre,
characters 6–7 of the TCGA barcode) and the outcome, to see what the main components are
associated with. Patients flagged in previous steps are circled in red.

```{r}
pca_df <- data.frame(sample        = rownames(X_filt),
                     PC1 = pca$x[, 1], PC2 = pca$x[, 2], PC3 = pca$x[, 3],
                     sample_median = sample_stats$sample_median[match(rownames(X_filt), sample_stats$sample)],
                     zeros         = rowMeans(X_filt == 0),
                     zk            = zk[rownames(X_filt)],
                     n_extreme     = n_extreme[rownames(X_filt)],
                     centre        = substr(rownames(X_filt), 6, 7),   # tissue source site
                     stage         = clin[rownames(X_filt), "outcome_p.stage"])
pca_df$flag <- pca_df$zk < -2 | pca_df$n_extreme > fence

# Helper: PCA scatter coloured by any variable (red circles = flagged patients)
plot_pca_by <- function(df, var, x = "PC1", y = "PC2") {
  p <- ggplot(df, aes(.data[[x]], .data[[y]], colour = .data[[var]])) +
    geom_point(size = 2.3, alpha = 0.85) +
    geom_point(data = subset(df, flag), shape = 21, size = 4.3,
               colour = "#D73027", stroke = 1) +
    labs(title = sprintf("PCA coloured by %s", var),
         subtitle = "Red circles = patients flagged in previous steps",
         x = sprintf("%s (%.1f%%)", x, 100 * var_exp[as.integer(sub("PC", "", x))]),
         y = sprintf("%s (%.1f%%)", y, 100 * var_exp[as.integer(sub("PC", "", y))]),
         colour = var) +
    theme_qc()
  if (is.numeric(df[[var]])) p + scale_colour_viridis_c() else p
}
```

## Stage and main genes of the components

The PCA coloured by pathological stage shows whether the main sources of variation in the
expression data are related to the outcome. The table lists the 10 genes with the largest
absolute loadings in the first three components, i.e. the genes that drive them.

```{r}
plot_pca_by(pca_df, "stage")                              # outcome

# Top 10 genes (absolute loadings) of the first three components
top_load <- function(pc, n = 10) {
  l <- pca$rotation[, pc]
  names(l[order(-abs(l))][1:n])
}
data.frame(PC1 = top_load(1), PC2 = top_load(2), PC3 = top_load(3))
```

## Association with QC metrics and centre

Spearman correlations between the first five components and the QC metrics: a strong
correlation with a QC metric would indicate that a component captures a technical effect. The
Kruskal–Wallis test checks whether the components differ between tissue source sites (centres
with at least 3 patients), which would indicate a **centre (batch) effect**.

```{r}
n_pc <- 5
round(cor(pca$x[, 1:n_pc],
          pca_df[, c("sample_median", "zeros", "zk", "n_extreme")],
          method = "spearman"), 2)

# Kruskal-Wallis test of each PC by centre (centres with at least 3 patients)
big_centres <- names(which(table(pca_df$centre) >= 3))
in_big      <- pca_df$centre %in% big_centres
data.frame(PC = paste0("PC", 1:n_pc),
           p_centre = sapply(1:n_pc, function(i)
             signif(kruskal.test(pca$x[in_big, i] ~ factor(pca_df$centre[in_big]))$p.value, 2)))

ggplot(subset(pca_df, in_big), aes(reorder(centre, PC3, FUN = stats::median), PC3)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey85", outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 1.5, colour = "#2C7FB8") +
  labs(title = "PC3 by tissue source site",
       subtitle = "Centres with at least 3 patients",
       x = "Centre", y = "PC3") +
  theme_qc() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

## Sensitivity to the most atypical patient

The PCA is repeated without the patient with the lowest connectivity. If the loadings with and
without this patient are almost identical (absolute correlations close to 1; the sign of a
component is arbitrary), this patient does not drive the PCA.

```{r}
most_atypical <- names(which.min(zk))
most_atypical

pca_wo <- prcomp(X_filt[rownames(X_filt) != most_atypical, ], center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)
data.frame(PC = paste0("PC", 1:n_pc),
           abs_cor_loadings = round(abs(diag(cor(pca$rotation[, 1:n_pc],
                                                 pca_wo$rotation[, 1:n_pc]))), 3))
rm(pca_wo); gc()
```

# QC summary per patient

Patients flagged in at least one step (distribution, connectivity, extreme values). They are
**flagged, not removed**: downstream analyses can be repeated with and without them.

```{r}
qc_table <- data.frame(
  patient           = rownames(X_filt),
  flag_distribution = sample_stats$flag[match(rownames(X_filt), sample_stats$sample)],
  flag_connectivity = zk[rownames(X_filt)] < -2,
  flag_extreme      = n_extreme[rownames(X_filt)] > fence
)
qc_table$n_flags <- rowSums(qc_table[, -1])
qc_flagged <- qc_table[qc_table$n_flags > 0, ]
qc_flagged[order(-qc_flagged$n_flags), ]
```

# Summary

- **`r sum(remove)` genes were removed** (not expressed, or low expression with frequent zeros), and **`r ncol(X_filt)` genes are kept** for the models.
- **No patient was removed.** `r nrow(qc_flagged)` patients were flagged in at least one step and are kept, as their atypical profiles can be biological.
- The PCA shows whether the main structure of the data is related to the outcome, to QC metrics or to the centre; a centre effect should be kept in mind when interpreting the models.

# Save

The filtered data and the QC parameters are written by the R script `02_qc_rnaseq.R`. In this
report the code is shown but **not run**, so that knitting does not overwrite the processed data
(nor the model cache that depends on them). Patients are saved in rows, with a patientID column
as in the other datasets.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
path.x <- "./data/processed"
dir.create(path.x, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

rna_df <- data.frame(X_filt, check.names = FALSE)
rna_df$patientID <- rownames(rna_df)
rna_df <- rna_df[, c(ncol(rna_df), 1:(ncol(rna_df) - 1))]   # patientID as first column

saveRDS(rna_df, file.path(path.x, "rna.train.filtered.rds"))          # filtered genes, log2(CPM + 1)

# Parameters estimated on the training set, to apply the same filtering to the test set
saveRDS(list(kept_genes = colnames(X_filt),   # genes kept after filtering
             nz_cut     = nz_cut,             # threshold of the non-zero mean
             filter_log = filter_log,         # reason for removal of each gene
             qc_flagged = qc_flagged),        # patients flagged in the QC
        file.path(path.x, "rna_qc_params.rds"))

gc()
```
